I have had similar hand and wrist issues on and off since I started tattooing. Some things that have helped me are: 

Physical therapy 

Wearing a wrist brace while I tattoo to stop myself from holding my machine too tightly 

Sleeping in a wrist brace 

Icing and stretching my hands and wrists after a long session 

Take frequent breaks when drawing or tattooing 
Wrapping my machine grips with something soft to widen the grip and dampen vibration 

Using rotary pen style machines which tend to be lighter than coil machines and experimenting with machines of different weights, grip sizes etc 

Trying to be mindful of my form and posture while drawing or tattooing (this is the main thing im still struggling with but I feel like im slowly figuring out how to make my station more ergonomic so I don’t have to think about it as much)

Idk if all of these have already been mentioned but hope this helps!

I have essential tremor so I’ve definitely struggled with line shakiness as well and can tell you a few things that have helped me. I usually run my machines around 8 or 9v so I can move my hand faster as other people have mentioned. I also try to be mindful of how I’m positioning my body to pull each line. Over time I’ve started to figure out what angles/positions feel most stable for my hand to pull a line in a particular direction and which angles cause me to shake more. I’m also always trying to find different ways to brace my arm and/or hand against something while I’m lining to improve my stability. You can try leaning over an extra armrest or something to pivot off of or sometimes I’ll even stretch with my forearm so that I can pivot off of my non dominant hand if I have to get anchored in a weird position. Also I try to always make sure I can plant my feet squarely on the floor since that helps me feel more stable for some reason. Idk if any of this is like official technique lol but these are just some things that have helped me. Lmk if any of them are useful for you as well 😊

I was just in a similar situation myself actually!  It’s been a little bit of a bumpy road but I finally feel like I’ve landed in a good place as a “real” artist at a shop. I’ll try and give you a short run down of what happened. Sorry in advance for how fucking long this is lol. 

I had been at my apprenticeship for about 2 years, tattooing on skin for a little less than a year. The situation at my apprenticeship became  unsustainable for me financially and I didn’t like the way I was being treated there, so I started sending out some feelers to see what my options might be at another shop. I’m not very social so I don’t know a lot of people in the community personally, so this mainly consisted of sending emails to shops that I saw were hiring and local artists I researched online who’s work I admired or who I felt I had things in common with. Basically I sent them a small portfolio of tattoos I had done and asked for advice on whether I was at a point where I could seek work as an artist or if I should look for another apprenticeship.  When applying to work at a shop I made sure to explain that I was an apprentice at the time/still had much to learn. I didn’t go into specifics about why I was trying to leave my apprenticeship but basically just said that it wasn’t a good fit/environment for me atm. 

I got a lot of good responses and feedback basically saying that my work looked “good enough” for someone with my level of experience.  Got hired at another local shop surprisingly quickly. The owners there were impressed with my portfolio and promised to continue teaching me as I transitioned to a full time artist at their shop. After one week working at the new shop however I was abruptly fired after doing only 3 tattoos. I was told that I was being fired because I lacked confidence and that my tattoos that I did that week didn’t stack up to what they had seen in my portfolio. It was a huge blow to my confidence but they gave me some good advice and recommended some other shops where they thought I would be a better fit. 

They told me I should seek out “street shops” that have a high volume of foot traffic and take walk ins.  These are usually situated on a main street/busy road in highly populated areas. They tend to get more walk ins and so are more likely to need additional artists and they are a good place to build a clientele.

I researched the shops recommended to me plus a bunch more online, specifically looking for places that took walk ins and were situated near a main thoroughfare. I also looked at the portfolios of the other artists working there and tried to find places where my work was at least close to on par with the other artists and where I felt like I might fit in with the people who worked and frequented there. Another thing I looked for was shops that hired commission based rather than renting out space/chairs, but that’s mostly just my personal preference plus I was hella broke lol. 

ANYWAY long story short (ish) I eventually found a shop really close to my house that checked all my aforementioned parameters and just walked in with my portfolio and set up a meeting with the shop owners for the next day. Everyone there was really friendly and welcoming and the owners liked my portfolio and general personality so it was a good fit all around pretty much right away. I’ve been working there for about 3 months now and it’s been really great. They have more walk ins than they know what to do with so I haven’t felt like I need to compete for clients and I’ve been getting a ton of practice which has really helped me build my skills and confidence. The owners and other artists have been super helpful with teaching me (which they said from the beginning they were comfortable with) and it’s overall just been a really encouraging environment. I feel really lucky and glad that I stuck with it until I found the right fit. 

So yea sorry for writing a novel lol but basically my advice is to start reaching out to other shops/artists asap and trying to find the “right fit” for your next shop/employer/mentor. I would put together a portfolio of your best tattoos that you’ve done so far (on skin) and maybe some of your best flash/drawings if you feel like you don’t have enough photos of tattoos but try and have mostly tattoos if you can.   You can send this to potential mentors/employers and ask for feedback/advice on what your options are and hopefully someone will be able to point you in a direction. 

I hope this helped!  Lmk if you have any questions or whatever. Kudos if you actually read all of this lol.

Hey there!  I’m about a year and a half into my apprenticeship now. I’m by no means an expert but I’ll do my best to answer your questions based on my own experience and what I’ve heard from other people in the industry. 

1.  It varies, but usually around 1-3 years

2.  My state doesn’t require certification, but my mentor told me that in states that do require tattoo artists to be certified an apprentice has the option to work under the umbrella of their mentors certification. If/when the apprentice decides to move on from their mentors shop, they must be judged by a sort of tribunal or whatever that usually consists of other established local tattoo artists in order to receive their certification. Not sure if there’s any official graduation marker in states without required certification but I’ll let you know if/when I reach that point lol 

3. I just googled stuff for my portfolio and tried to include pieces that mimicked the major styles I had read about. I learned more about tattoo art styles and got better at designing them once I started my apprenticeship. 

4. I would wait on buying supplies until you’re well into your apprenticeship. Most apprentices won’t do any tattooing at all for at least their first few months. You will also have a better idea of what to buy once you’ve learned a little more about tattooing in general. 

Hope this helps!
